chokepoints.name: Strait of Hormuz
chokepoints.normal: ~85 ships a day (IMF PortWatch); ~125 large vessels a day (Kpler)
chokepoints.latest: 4 ships on 18 Oct, about 5% of typical (IMF PortWatch)
chokepoints.carries: ~20% of world crude oil and LNG
chokepoints.note: Effectively closed since the US-Iran war began on 28 Feb. Tracked ships are near zero, but Kpler says some crude still moves on tankers with trackers switched off. Attacks on ships rose in October.
chokepoints.traffic: 4 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 4, 96% below the 2023 average of 96 a day (IMF PortWatch)

chokepoints.name: Bab el-Mandeb
chokepoints.normal: about 2,300 ships a month before the Houthi crisis (estimate from Lloyd's List figure of -47%)
chokepoints.carries: ~12% of world trade, ~11% of seaborne oil, ~8% of LNG
chokepoints.note: Houthis took Mocha and Perim island in September 2026 and now hold Yemen's whole Red Sea coast. A Chinese-run container ship was fired on off Yemen on 7 Oct.
chokepoints.traffic: 32 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 26, 65% below the 2023 average of 75 a day (IMF PortWatch)

chokepoints.name: Suez Canal
chokepoints.normal: about 2,000 ships a month before the Red Sea crisis (estimate from -39% figure)
chokepoints.latest: 1,228 ships in Sept 2026, busiest month since Dec 2023
chokepoints.carries: Main Asia-Europe shortcut; key for Saudi oil shipped from Yanbu
chokepoints.note: Traffic is recovering but still 39% below pre-crisis levels. Many container lines still go round Africa. Egypt lost about $7bn of canal revenue in 2023-24.
chokepoints.traffic: 43 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 44, 40% below the 2023 average of 74 a day (IMF PortWatch)

chokepoints.name: Cape of Good Hope (diversion route)
chokepoints.normal: Not a chokepoint; normal traffic figures not confirmed
chokepoints.latest: Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd moved three services back to Red Sea routes in Sept 2026
chokepoints.carries: Most Asia-Europe container traffic avoiding the Red Sea
chokepoints.note: Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd and CMA CGM rerouted around Africa in March 2026. The detour adds 10-14 days. The 112% figure has no clear baseline, so treat it with care.
chokepoints.traffic: 78 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 86, 75% above the 2023 average of 49 a day (IMF PortWatch)

chokepoints.name: Strait of Malacca
chokepoints.latest: 21 armed robberies in H1 2026, down 74% on a year earlier
chokepoints.carries: Main route for Gulf and Atlantic energy to East Asia
chokepoints.note: Open with no major disruption reported. The eastbound Singapore Strait remains the main spot for robberies at sea.
chokepoints.traffic: 227 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 215, close to the 2023 average of 219 a day (IMF PortWatch)

chokepoints.name: Panama Canal
chokepoints.latest: 33 slots a day from 15 Oct; Neopanamax draft 49 ft
chokepoints.carries: Key route for US LNG and goods to Asia
chokepoints.note: A drier rainy season cut daily slots in September. Some limits eased in late September. Demand from US LNG tankers rose sharply after the Hormuz closure.
chokepoints.traffic: 29 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 28, 13% below the 2023 average of 32 a day (IMF PortWatch)

chokepoints.name: Turkish Straits (Bosporus)
chokepoints.latest: Drone-damaged tanker ran aground off Istanbul on 16 Oct
chokepoints.carries: Russian and Kazakh oil, Black Sea grain
chokepoints.note: The straits are open, but Russia and Ukraine are both attacking ships in the Black Sea. Some tankers use nets and tyres as makeshift drone defences.
chokepoints.traffic: 58 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 47, 52% below the 2023 average of 97 a day (IMF PortWatch)

chokepoints.name: Strait of Gibraltar
chokepoints.latest: No disruption reported; Tanger Med expected more calls from rerouted ships
chokepoints.carries: Atlantic-Mediterranean gateway; ships coming round Africa
chokepoints.note: No disruption reported. Ships sent round Africa reach the Mediterranean this way, so ports like Tanger Med expected more traffic.
chokepoints.traffic: 142 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 124, 15% below the 2023 average of 146 a day (IMF PortWatch)

chokepoints.name: Danish Straits
chokepoints.carries: About a third of Russia's seaborne oil exports
chokepoints.note: Open to shipping. Denmark checks 'shadow fleet' tankers anchoring off Skagen and can detain unsafe or uninsured ships.
chokepoints.traffic: 42 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 41, 9% below the 2023 average of 46 a day (IMF PortWatch, Øresund only)

chokepoints.name: Taiwan Strait
chokepoints.latest: China announced live-fire drills in 5 coastal zones from 15 Oct, none around Taiwan
chokepoints.carries: Major East Asia container and energy route
chokepoints.note: Open. China's October 2026 no-sail zones run from the South China Sea to Liaoning, with the closest off Zhejiang. No wider shipping impact has been reported.
chokepoints.traffic: 230 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 227, 6% below the 2023 average of 242 a day (IMF PortWatch)

chokepoints.name: English Channel / Dover Strait
chokepoints.latest: UK boarded the sanctioned tanker Smyrtos in June 2026
chokepoints.carries: One of the world's busiest shipping lanes; Russian Baltic oil exports
chokepoints.note: Open. In June 2026 Royal Marines boarded a sanctioned 'shadow fleet' tanker in the Channel and held it off Portland. Britain has sanctioned over 500 such ships.
chokepoints.traffic: 173 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 175, close to the 2023 average of 176 a day (IMF PortWatch)

chokepoints.name: Kerch Strait
chokepoints.normal: Ferry and tanker link between Russia and occupied Crimea
chokepoints.latest: Ukraine says a drone campaign cut ferry capacity by 75% (July 2026)
chokepoints.carries: Supplies to Crimea; Russian oil and products
chokepoints.note: Drone strikes in 2026 hit ferries, fuel sites and ports around Kerch and Port Kavkaz. Risk is expected to stay high for the rest of 2026.
chokepoints.traffic: 0 ships on 18 Oct, 7-day average 0, 100% below the 2023 average of 9 a day (IMF PortWatch)

lanes.name: Asia – Europe via Suez
lanes.note: Container transits through Suez reached about 753,000 TEU a week in early October 2026, over half of pre-crisis levels per BIMCO and Clarksons (15 Oct). Recovery is still well below pre-crisis levels, and carrier routing depends on Houthi restraint near Bab el-Mandeb.

lanes.name: Asia – Europe round Africa
lanes.note: Where most big container lines now sail. The detour adds about 10–14 days and roughly 6,000 km.

lanes.name: Gulf oil to Asia
lanes.note: The world's busiest oil route, mostly shut since the Hormuz closure began on 28 Feb 2026.

lanes.name: Qatar LNG to Japan & Korea
lanes.note: Qatar's LNG exports are under force majeure and blocked by the Hormuz closure.

lanes.name: Gulf oil & gas to Europe
lanes.note: Blocked at Hormuz and exposed at Bab el-Mandeb.

lanes.name: Saudi Red Sea bypass (Yanbu)
lanes.note: Saudi crude piped across the desert to Yanbu now ships north through Suez, avoiding Hormuz.

lanes.name: UAE bypass (Fujairah)
lanes.note: The UAE pipes oil to Fujairah, outside Hormuz. The port has been attacked, so flows are uncertain.

lanes.name: Trans-Pacific
lanes.note: China and East Asia to the US West Coast. Open.

lanes.name: Asia – US East Coast via Panama
lanes.note: Panama Canal raised daily transit slots to 33 from 15 Oct 2026, up from 32 set on 15 Sep, as Gatun Lake levels improved. Capacity remains below normal levels.

lanes.name: Trans-Atlantic
lanes.note: Europe to the US East Coast. Open.

lanes.name: US LNG to Europe
lanes.note: Record US LNG exports are filling the gap left by Qatar.

lanes.name: US LNG to Asia via Panama
lanes.note: Asian buyers turned to US LNG after the Hormuz closure, adding pressure on the Panama Canal.

lanes.name: Russian oil from the Baltic (shadow fleet)
lanes.note: Much of it moves on ageing, often uninsured “shadow fleet” tankers. The EU lists about 673 of them.

lanes.name: Russian oil from the Black Sea
lanes.note: Tankers out of Novorossiysk face Ukrainian drone attacks and Western sanctions.

lanes.name: Ukrainian grain from Odesa
lanes.note: Ukraine's export corridor keeps running despite Russian strikes on ports and ships.

cables.name: PEACE
cables.route: France – Egypt – Kenya (and on to Pakistan)

cableIncidents.name: Gulf cables (FIG, Falcon, AAE-1, Gulf Bridge International)
cableIncidents.note: No confirmed cuts in 2026. The Wall Street Journal reported Iran was weighing attacks on Gulf cables. Repair ships cannot safely reach the area.

cableIncidents.name: Vietnam international cables (not named)
cableIncidents.note: Four separate cable faults disrupted Vietnam's international traffic. The cause was not stated. The date is when the report was listed.

cableIncidents.name: SEA-ME-WE 5 (Pakistan)
cableIncidents.note: A fault on SMW5 slowed internet in Pakistan. The operator called it a technical fault. The cause and the fault's location were not given.

cableIncidents.name: Taiwan-Matsu Cable 3 (Dongyin-Beigan)
cableIncidents.note: Partly broken. Taiwan suspects a Chinese salvage barge damaged it while removing a grounded fishing boat. The crew were questioned, and service continues while repairs are arranged.

cableIncidents.name: BCS East (Latvia-Lithuania, Arelion)
cableIncidents.note: Damaged a few km from Liepaja, Latvia. Reports say a ship changed course over the cable. Latvian police are investigating, and no cause has been confirmed.

cableIncidents.name: Elisa Helsinki-Tallinn cable + two Arelion cables
cableIncidents.note: Finland seized the cargo ship Fitburg, which is suspected of dragging its anchor, and detained its 14 crew. It was carrying sanctioned Russian steel. Legal proceedings opened in 2026.

cableIncidents.name: SMW4 and IMEWE (Red Sea, near Jeddah)
cableIncidents.note: The cuts slowed internet in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Pakistan and India and disrupted Microsoft Azure. No cause was established.

cableIncidents.name: Taiwan-Penghu No. 3 (TPKM-3)
cableIncidents.note: Damaged in 2025. A Taiwanese court jailed the Chinese captain for three years and ordered about $560,000 in restitution.

cableIncidents.name: Two Taiwan-Matsu cables
cableIncidents.note: One cable was cut and one badly faulty, affecting about 14,000 islanders, who switched to microwave backup. The cause was not stated.

cableIncidents.name: Trans-Pacific Express segment near Keelung
cableIncidents.note: Taiwan suspects the Hong Kong-owned freighter Shunxin-39 dragged its anchor over the cable. Traffic was rerouted with no outage.

sanctions.note: UN sanctions returned on 27 Sept 2025 (snapback). The US has made over 1,000 designations, including 180+ tankers and China's Hengli refinery. It briefly allowed buying Iranian oil at sea in March-April 2026.

The EU's 21st package (23 July 2026) targets about 673 shadow-fleet tankers and 94 banks. The EU added 1,569 listings on 12 Oct 2026. On 16 Oct 2026 the US waived Graham Act sanctions and tariffs on Russia; Russian diesel sanctions were waived until April 2027.
UN sanctions remain. An 11-nation monitoring team said in Sept 2026 that North Korean workers abroad earned $450-800m in 2025, breaking UN rules. Pyongyang rejected the report.

The US repealed the Caesar Act on 18 Dec 2025 and rescinded Syria's state sponsor of terrorism designation on 24 Aug 2026. The US removed Syria from its ITAR arms-denial list on 1 Oct 2026. Targeted sanctions remain on Assad associates, human rights abusers, Captagon traffickers and Iran proxies.

The long-standing US embargo continues. New Cuba Sanctions Regulations took effect 30 Sept 2026 under EO 14404, adding blocking powers and ending the U-turn licence. The US oil blockade began in January 2026; a Russian tanker delivered fuel in late March.

After the US seized Maduro on 3 Jan 2026, it eased oil, gas and mining sanctions through licences. The core orders remain, and most dealings with the government are still banned. EU measures not checked.
In March 2026 the US delisted the potash firms Belaruskali and BPC and lifted its sovereign-debt ban. EU sanctions on potash, banks and debt remain much stricter.
In April 2026 the EU extended its arms embargo, asset freezes and travel bans on 105 people and 22 organisations until at least May 2027. Current US measures were not checked.
Sanctions target the Taliban rather than the whole economy. In March 2026 the US named Afghanistan a 'State Sponsor of Wrongful Detention', with no specific measures announced.

exportControls.note: April 2025 licence rules for seven heavy rare earths still apply. Wider October 2025 rules are suspended until 10 Nov 2026; Washington said in late Sept 2026 the truce runs to 10 Jan 2027, not yet matched by Beijing.

exportControls.what: Gallium, germanium, antimony, superhard materials (to US)
exportControls.note: China's ban on these exports to the US is suspended until 27 Nov 2026. Its December 2024 ban on dual-use items for US military users still stands.

exportControls.what: Advanced AI chips to China (Nvidia H200, AMD MI325X)
exportControls.note: Since January 2026, the US has licensed sales case by case with an effective 25% fee and volume caps. More advanced chips stay restricted. Reports say Beijing loosened its H200 import block; Nvidia's April 2026 filing says it lacks approval from both governments.

exportControls.what: Defence ban on Chinese-origin rare earth magnets
exportControls.note: From January 2027, the US defence supply chain may not use Chinese-origin rare earth elements or permanent magnets.

pipelines.name: East-West Pipeline (Petroline)
pipelines.note: Saudi Arabia's main way around Hormuz, with 7m barrels a day capacity. It pumped 5.8m b/d on 6 Oct, after drone strikes in September forced a brief shutdown.

pipelines.name: Habshan-Fujairah (ADCOP)
pipelines.note: The UAE's Hormuz bypass, about 1.5m b/d capacity. Fujairah port has been attacked. Current flow rates were not confirmed. A second pipeline is being fast-tracked for 2027.

pipelines.name: Iraq-Turkey Pipeline (Kirkuk-Ceyhan)
pipelines.note: Iraq says exports via Ceyhan continue. A one-year Iraq-Turkey deal was signed in August, with initial capacity of 750,000 b/d. Actual flows were not confirmed and are hit by wartime shut-ins.

pipelines.name: Druzhba (southern branch)
pipelines.note: Flows have been halted several times by drone strikes on pumping stations. Deliveries to Hungary and Slovakia were reported back to normal in May 2026.

pipelines.name: Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC)
pipelines.note: Carries about 80% of Kazakhstan's oil exports. A naval drone hit one of three moorings in Nov 2025. Tanker strikes in July 2026 halted loadings until 27 July. CPC said the Tengiz-Novorossiysk pipeline resumed on 6 Oct 2026. Current capacity was not confirmed.

pipelines.name: TurkStream
pipelines.to: Turkey and SE Europe (Bulgaria, Serbia, Hungary)
pipelines.note: The last working route for Russian pipeline gas to Europe. Flows to Europe averaged 44.8m cubic metres a day in September 2026, down 13% on a year earlier.

pipelines.name: Nord Stream 1 and 2
pipelines.note: No gas has flowed since the 2022 blasts. In October 2026 the Kremlin commented on an upcoming trial over the sabotage.

pipelines.name: Power of Siberia
pipelines.note: Russia plans to send 50bn cubic metres of gas to China in 2026 via this line and Kazakhstan. The planned second line has been renamed 'Power of Baikal'.

lng.name: Ras Laffan (Qatar)
lng.note: Under force majeure. Iranian missiles knocked out about 17% of capacity. September exports of 1.6m t were under a quarter of pre-war levels, and October may fall to 0.6m t.

lng.name: Das Island (UAE)
lng.note: Capacity is 6m tonnes a year, inside Hormuz. ADNOC has no force majeure, but a few cargoes slipped out with trackers off. ADNOC Gas export volumes fell 53% in Q2.

lng.name: Sabine Pass / Golden Pass (US Gulf, Louisiana-Texas)
lng.note: US exports averaged a record 17.4bn cubic feet a day in H1 2026, up 23%. Golden Pass shipped its first cargo on 22 April. Exports to Asia more than doubled.

lng.name: Plaquemines LNG (US, Louisiana)
lng.note: Phase 1 cleared by FERC to enter service on 16 Oct 2026. Terminal exporting at full capacity, helping fill the gap left by Gulf LNG.

lng.name: Corpus Christi LNG (US, Texas)
lng.note: Stage 3's seventh train was completed on 28 Aug 2026, taking capacity above 25m tonnes a year.

lng.name: North West Shelf / Gorgon (Australia)
lng.note: Australia is expected to regain its place as the No. 2 LNG exporter in 2026. Higher prices from the Hormuz closure are lifting export income. Terminal-level volumes were not checked.

lng.name: Yamal LNG (Sabetta, Russia)
lng.note: The EU took a record 12.2m t in Jan-Sept 2026 despite a ban on short-term contracts from April. A full EU ban starts on 1 Jan 2027.

starlink.note: Widely used by Ukraine's military and public services. Since February 2026, only whitelisted, registered terminals work in Ukraine.
Sales to Russia are barred under US sanctions, but Russian forces used smuggled terminals, including on drones. SpaceX's whitelist cut them off in Ukraine in February 2026.
Starlink is outlawed. Users face up to 2 years in prison, distributors up to 5, and spying charges can carry death. Tens of thousands of terminals were smuggled in, and authorities jam the service.
In Darfur, smuggled terminals from Libya and Chad are the only link to the outside world, sold by the hour. Users fear their location can be tracked.
SpaceX disabled about 2,500 terminals at scam compounds in Oct 2025. Civil groups say later undeclared blocks hit Magway, Sagaing and Rakhine, cutting humanitarian users.
Israel approved Starlink in February 2024, at first only for a UAE field hospital in Gaza. Gaza use needs Israeli approval.
The recognised government licensed Starlink until 2029. The Houthis ban it in the north and threaten sellers, but smuggled kits are spreading.

Starlink got a licence in June 2025 but not final clearances. Security concerns reportedly held up commercial launch in 2026. As of 16 Oct 2026 no launch date is confirmed; SpaceX says its systems are ready.

Starlink has had provisional registration since March 2025. Satellite licensing framework was reported finalised in April 2026, but rules were still nearing completion in Oct 2026. The service has not launched.

Starlink is not licensed because of a 30% black ownership rule. A Dec 2025 policy direction lets equity-equivalent investment count, but the Act still needs amending as of Aug 2026. No licence has been issued.
Starlink is not registered in China. Since February 2026, merchant ships must switch off Starlink in Chinese waters and ports. China is building rival networks.
Starlink does not serve Taiwan. A July 2026 law lets regulators waive foreign ownership caps, and Taiwan is talking with OneWeb and Amazon for backup links.

blackouts.note: An 88-day nationwide blackout began with the US-Israeli strikes and was partly lifted in late May. Heavy filtering continues, WhatsApp is blocked, and more curbs are threatened.

blackouts.note: Repeated 50-minute nationwide shutdowns during school exams in August and September 2026. A separate regional shutdown has run since February 2025.
